title: Bigfoot doc drops bombshell on famous 1967 footage
excerpt: A new documentary is reigniting debate over one of the most famous mysteries in American folklore.
content:
Don Davis

Updated Sat, October 24, 2026 at 5:05 AM UTC

(NewsNation) — A new documentary is reigniting debate over one of the most famous mysteries in American folklore. Speaking with NewsNation's Jesse Weber, Marq Evans, director of "Capturing Bigfoot," said he initially set out to examine the legendary 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film, only to uncover a much deeper story about family, money and betrayal.

Evans told Weber the project evolved beyond the question of whether Bigfoot exists.

"The characters and everything that they went through to protect this footage, the money that was made off of it, the betrayals, the redemption, all these things that you want in a great film all came out in this story," he said.

Bigfoot hunter says proving corpse’s authenticity has been an uphill battle

Lost footage sheds new light on the legend behind Bigfoot

According to the "Capturing Bigfoot" official synopsis, the film revisits the famous footage captured by Roger Patterson in Northern California in 1967, a clip that has fueled decades of debate among believers and skeptics alike. The documentary centers on newly discovered 16mm footage that filmmakers say sheds new light on the story.

The film's producer, Tamir Ardon, said he was surprised by the massive financial ecosystem that grew around the Bigfoot legend. During the interview, Ardon described the phenomenon as a billion-dollar industry fueled by books, television shows, merchandise and tourism tied to the creature's enduring popularity.

Ardon said the filmmakers encountered believers from all walks of life during production. "There are really two sets of believers out there. There's the ones that approach it from a scientific standpoint. And then there's the ones that we've really come to understand that this is a religion to them," he told Weber.

Cluster of Bigfoot sightings reported in Northeast Ohio

The film's emotional core focuses on Clint Patterson, the son of Roger Patterson. Evans said Clint spent much of his life carrying the weight of his father's legacy before ultimately deciding to participate in the documentary and discuss what he knew about the famous footage.

"He never asked to live with this story his entire life," Evans said of Clint. "He's always worshipped his father. He still does, but he's known for a long time the truth about this story."

'...the Bigfoot in this 1967 footage is not a real Bigfoot in our conclusion.'

According to Evans, the documentary began after Teresa Brooks contacted him in 2022 about a reel of film discovered in a family safe.

That discovery launched an investigation that eventually became the centerpiece of the project and what filmmakers describe as a major revelation about the Bigfoot phenomenon.

While the documentary reaches a controversial conclusion about the Patterson footage, Ardon said the filmmakers were not trying to attack believers.

Bigfoot sighting in Central Pennsylvania ‘very credible,’ researcher says

"We're not looking to kill Santa Claus," he said. "Bigfoot might exist out there. It's just that the Bigfoot in this 1967 footage is not a real Bigfoot in our conclusion."

The documentary arrives as interest in Bigfoot remains high across the country. NewsNation has previously reported on alleged sightings, investigations and even purported Bigfoot remains, underscoring how the mystery continues to captivate believers despite decades of debate over the creature's existence.

According to the official website for "Capturing Bigfoot," the documentary explores how a mystery that began with less than a minute of film grew into a cultural obsession spanning generations. The film is available through Prime Video and continues to spark debate among Bigfoot enthusiasts across the country.
